## Developmental sensitivity

Our goal for the LEVANTE core tasks is that they are sensitive to developmental change. In cross-sectional data, the age-gradients provide an approximation of how sensitive a task is to developmental differences and may, when longitudinal data are available, capture within-person change. We reiterate here that we do not believe absolute differences between sites are interpretable, because of confounding due to differences in sampling, recruitment, and administration of the tasks; our interest instead is in within-site developmental change.

Across all nine tasks, ability scores were higher at older ages at all sites, indicating robust positive age gradients (see @fig-age-trends). This pattern was particularly pronounced for Math, Vocabulary, and Shape Rotation. Age gradients were broadly similar across sites: the panels suggest parallel developmental gradients in ability, with systematic shifts in mean ability but little evidence that the age-related slope differs markedly by site.

To quantify the age gradients, we fit ordinary least-squares models for each task predicting scaled ability scores (IRT units) from age with site fixed effects and an age by site interaction, allowing slopes to vary by site. Using the `marginaleffects` package [@marginaleffects], we extracted marginal estimates of age gradients. As summarized in @tbl-age-effects and @fig-age-slopes, age-related gradients were positive for all tasks and sites, indicating that older children on average performed better on every measure.

For ease of interpretation, we calculated the zero-order correlations between age and IRT ability scores for each site. As seen in the right side of @tbl-age-effects, these correlations were almost uniformly positive (_r_ = `r age_cor_range[1]` to `r age_cor_range[2]`, with the exception of Same & Different in uniandes-co-rural, which has small sample size), of moderate magnitude across tasks, and broadly similar across sites. In sum, the results of the age-based analyses suggest that the tasks are sensitive to age-related differences and are likely suitable for deployment in longitudinal studies of developmental change.


## Reliability 

One goal for the LEVANTE core tasks is strong reliability both within an individual administration (across test items) and across multiple administrations separated in time. We report on each of these. 

### Empirical reliability
{{< include _06-reliability.qmd >}}

Empirical marginal reliability, an IRT-based analogue to Cronbach's $\alpha$, quantifies the proportion of true-score variance captured by a test based on the item information function [@thissen2001test]. Unlike classical coefficients, which assume uniform measurement precision across the ability range, IRT reliability allows that precision varies across $\theta$ and estimates overall reliability by integrating information across the population distribution [@embretson2013]. In multi-group IRT models, empirical reliability is computed separately for each site-specific sub-model. @tbl-task-rxx reports empirical reliabilities for each task and site from the best-fitting IRT model. Reliabilities were largely acceptable (>.60) [@nunnally1978psychometric], with the exception of the Stories task, the only task falling below this threshold in any site, and then only slightly (.56 at mpieva-de and .58 at uniandes-co-bogota, against .68 and .80 at the other two sites). Reliabilities did not differ substantially by age group nor by sex (see @tbl-task-subgroup-rxx). The Same and Different estimate for uniandes-co-rural rests on only 20 administrations and should be treated as imprecise.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task-rxx
#| dependson: load-rxx
#| tbl-cap: "Empirical reliabilities for each task by site or language."
#| ft.arraystretch: 0.9

flextable(task_rxx) |>
  hline(~task == "" & lead(task) != "",
        border = officer::fp_border(color = "lightgrey", width = 0.75)) |>
  # align(align = c("left", "left", "right", "right", "right"), part = "all") |>
  fontsize(size = 10, part = "all") |>
  set_header_labels("task" = "Task", "group_label" = "Group",
                    "itemtype" = "Model", "invariance" = "Invariance",
                    "n" = "N", "empirical_rxx" = "Empirical reliability") |>
  align_text_col() |>
  autofit()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-task-subgroup-rxx
#| tbl-cap: "Empirical reliabilities for each task by age group and by sex."
#| ft.arraystretch: 1

subgroup_cols <- tibble(nm = names(subgroup_rxx)) |>
  separate_wider_delim(nm, names = c("r1", "r2"), delim = "-",
                       too_few = "align_start", cols_remove = FALSE) |>
  mutate(r1 = r1 |> replace_values("itemtype" ~ "model") |>
           str_replace_all("_", " ") |> str_to_sentence(),
         r2 = r2 |> str_replace("_", "–"))

flextable(subgroup_rxx) |>
  split_header(sep = "-") |>
  set_header_df(mapping = subgroup_cols, key = "nm") |>
  merge_h(part = "header") |>
  hline(i = 1, border = gray_border, part = "header") |>
  hline(i = 1, j = 1:3, border = officer::fp_border(color = "white"), part = "header") |>
  theme_apa() |>
  padding(1) |>
  align_text_col() |>
  autofit()
```

\clearpage

### Test-retest reliability
{{< include _07-retest.qmd >}}

We were also interested in the extent to which the LEVANTE tasks yield a consistent rank ordering of ability across repeated assessments separated by a delay of several months. Under classical test theory assumptions, test--retest correlations provide an estimate of score reliability that complements the empirical reliabilities reported above [@kline2013handbook]. The mpieva-de pilot site was able to re-administer tasks to a subset of their original participant group with a retest interval of either 3 months (group 1) or 7 months (group 2) approximately. We used this re-administration as an opportunity to collect data with computer adaptive versions of many of the tasks (Sentence Understanding, Pattern Matching, Shape Rotation, Math, and Vocabulary); see below for further details of computer adaptive versions. In addition, for several tasks (Math, Stories, Pattern Matching), we used this opportunity to gather item data about new groups of retest items, designed to test the same content as the original items while differing in their specific details, such as the particular numbers, names, or pictures used. For the other tasks, we retested using the same items. 

@fig-retest shows the relations between time 1 and time 2 scores. Across individual tasks, retest sample sizes ranged from N = `r min(trt$n)` to N = `r max(trt$n)`; the relatively lower number of repeat administrations for Sentence Understanding reflects an error in which this task was not sent to younger children. Children in the test–retest subsample were very similar in age to those in the overall mpieva-de pilot sample. The overall sample (n = `r age_comp$gen$n`) had a mean age of `r age_comp$gen$mean_age` years (SD = `r age_comp$gen$sd_age`), whereas the test–retest subsample (n = `r age_comp$trt$n`) had a mean age of `r age_comp$trt$mean_age` years (SD = `r age_comp$trt$sd_age`), a difference of approximately `r age_comp$gen$mean_age - age_comp$trt$mean_age` years (~`r 12 * (age_comp$gen$mean_age - age_comp$trt$mean_age)` months). Each figure panel also shows the test-retest correlation and sample size for the corresponding task. Retest correlations ranged from $r =$ `{r} trt_range[1]` to $r =$ `{r} trt_range[2]`, with Math showing the highest rank-order stability. Retest correlations of this magnitude indicate substantial stability in the rank ordering of ability over three to seven months. They should not, however, be read as pure reliability estimates: the interval allows real developmental change, and three tasks were retested with newly written items whose difficulty may not have matched the originals exactly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-retest
#| fig-cap: "Test-retest correlations per task (in mpieva-de data)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 9

ggplot(retest_wide_coretask, aes(run_1, run_2, colour = mean_age)) +
  facet_nested_wrap(vars(task_category, task), scales = "free", axes = "x",
                    nest_line = element_line(), solo_line = TRUE) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_label(data = trt, inherit.aes = FALSE,
             aes(label = sprintf("r = %.2f", test_retest_r)),
             x = -Inf, y = Inf, hjust = "inward", vjust = "inward",
             size = 3, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0) +
  geom_label(data = trt, inherit.aes = FALSE,
             aes(label = sprintf("N = %s", n)),
             x = Inf, y = -Inf, hjust = "inward", vjust = "inward",
             size = 3, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0) +
  scale_colour_viridis_b(limits = c(5, 13), end = 0.95) +
  guides(colour = guide_coloursteps()) +
  labs(x = "Score 1", y = "Score 2", colour = "Age (years)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", aspect.ratio = 1)
```

\clearpage

## Validity
{{< include _08-sem.qmd >}}

Validity is not a property of a task itself but of the interpretations placed on the scores it yields, and it is judged by how far those interpretations are supported by theory and by accumulated empirical evidence for the particular use proposed [@aera2014standards]. Validation is therefore cumulative rather than settled by any single analysis, and different strands of evidence bear on different aspects of the question: the internal structure of a battery speaks to whether its tasks cohere as the intended constructs, while relations to external criteria speak to whether scores behave as those constructs should. We report both strands below.

Assessment of validity for the core tasks was challenging, in part because of the precise issues that motivated us to create the task battery in the first place. No readily available, internationalized measures existed to compare to many of our tasks. Thus, for validation evidence, we rely on the overall construct structure of the core task battery as well as the relations to our gold standard measures for literacy (ROAR-Word, ROAR-Sentence and ROAR-Phoneme) and executive function (MEFS).

### Construct validity

We assessed construct validity using a structural equation model (SEM) specifying three first‐order latent factors—Reasoning, Executive Function, and Language—with each factor measured by its respective tasks and allowed to covary with Math and Stories (see @fig-semplot-core-tasks). Math and Stories were each measured by a single task, so neither admits a conventional multi-indicator latent variable. We therefore modelled Math as a single-indicator latent variable, fixing its residual variance at 1 -- *r*~xx~ using the task's empirical marginal reliability (*r*~xx~ = .92, averaged across sites weighted by *N*); because the scores entering the model are standardised, this expresses the construct net of measurement error on the same scale. We did not impose the equivalent correction on Stories, whose reliability is both lower and considerably more variable across sites (.56--.80 in @tbl-task-rxx). Applying the same correction at Stories' pooled reliability yields an inadmissible solution: the Language--Stories correlation rises to .97 and the latent covariance matrix is no longer positive definite. The correction is admissible only if Stories' reliability is assumed to be at least .64, which exceeds both its pooled estimate and the values observed at three of the four sites; at the lowest site value (.56) the implied correlation exceeds unity. Stories is therefore retained as an observed endogenous outcome, and its coefficients should be read as attenuated by measurement error. Age was specified to predict each of the latent factors, including Math, as well as the observed Stories outcome.

```{r}
#| label: fig-semplot-core-tasks
#| dependson: sem-g-plot
#| fig-cap: "Structural Equation Model for core tasks.
#| *Note: Ovals represent latent factors; rectangles represent observed variables. Blue fill indicates latent factors, orange indicates the age predictor, and grey indicates observed indicators and outcomes. Green arrows represent factor loadings; blue arrows represent regression paths; grey dashed double-headed arrows represent residual variances and covariances (error terms). Values on paths are standardised coefficients.*"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 9

plot_sem_clear(g)
```
\clearpage

Overall model fit `r fit_verdict(fitMeasures(fit_cov_age)["cfi"], fitMeasures(fit_cov_age)["rmsea"])` (CFI $\geq$ .95, RMSEA $\leq$ .06) [@hu1999cutoff], CFI: `r round(fitMeasures(fit_cov_age)["cfi"], 3)`, RMSEA: `r round(fitMeasures(fit_cov_age)["rmsea"], 3)`, RMSEA p-value: `r pval_fmt(fitMeasures(fit_cov_age)["rmsea.pvalue"])`. Factor loadings supported the intended three-factor structure (convergent validity), and age showed positive associations with each domain. The high inter-factor correlations indicate that much of the variance is shared across domains. 


The three factors are strongly intercorrelated: Reasoning with Executive Function *r* = `r round(fc("reasoning ef", "r"), 2)`, 95% CI `r fc_ci("reasoning ef")`, Reasoning with Language `r round(fc("reasoning language", "r"), 2)` `r fc_ci("reasoning language")`, and Executive Function with Language `r round(fc("ef language", "r"), 2)` `r fc_ci("ef language")`.


\clearpage

Whether these high correlations reflect a single broad dimension or genuinely distinct but closely related domains is a question of factor structure that this pilot cannot settle, and that we take up in dedicated work in preparation. We therefore report the correlations here without adjudicating between those interpretations.

This pattern of high correlations does not appear to be an artifact of the pilot sample's site composition: repeating the correlated three-factor model on 200 equal-size-per-site subsamples produced highly consistent factor correlations (Reasoning–EF, Reasoning–Language, EF–Language all within $\pm.02$ of the full-sample estimates on average; @tbl-subsample-robustness, @fig-subsample-robustness in the appendix), and the same qualitative pattern held, albeit more noisily, within the two individual sites for which within-site model estimation was stable (@tbl-within-site-robustness).

### External validity

To assess external validity for the executive function tasks, we fit a single-factor executive function model with Hearts and Flowers, Memory, Same and Different, and the external measure, the Minnesota Executive Function Scale (MEFS), as indicators (@fig-semplot-ef). The model is a measurement model only; age is not included as a predictor, since the question here is whether the tasks and the external criterion mark out a common construct, and developmental effects are reported above. Model fit `r fit_verdict(fitMeasures(fit_ef)["cfi"], fitMeasures(fit_ef)["rmsea"])` (CFI $\geq$ .95, RMSEA $\leq$ .06) [@hu1999cutoff], CFI: `r round(fitMeasures(fit_ef)["cfi"], 3)`, RMSEA: `r round(fitMeasures(fit_ef)["rmsea"], 3)`, RMSEA p-value: `r pval_fmt(fitMeasures(fit_ef)["rmsea.pvalue"])`. Standardized loadings were moderate-to-strong: Hearts and Flowers = `r fmt(load_tab["hf"])`, Memory = `r fmt(load_tab["mg"])`, Same and Different = `r fmt(load_tab["sds"])`, MEFS = `r fmt(load_tab["mefs"])`, indicating that the MEFS aligns closely with the latent executive function construct.

```{r}
#| label: fig-semplot-ef
#| dependson: sem-ef-plot
#| fig-cap: "External validity evidence for Executive Function: SEM including the Minnesota Executive Function Scale (MEFS) as an external criterion measure.
#| *Note: The oval represents the latent factor and rectangles represent observed task scores. Green arrows show factor loadings. Values on paths are standardised coefficients.*"
#| fig-height: 4

plot_sem_clear(g_ef)
```

\clearpage

We ran a similar model to determine the external validity of the language and literacy measures (Sentence Understanding and Vocabulary) against ROAR tasks, including measures of Phonological Awareness (ROAR-Phoneme), Single Word Reading (ROAR-Word) and Sentence Reading Efficiency (ROAR-Sentence). We fit a single latent Language factor with ROAR tasks plus Sentence Understanding and Vocabulary as indicators, specified as a measurement model without age (@fig-semplot-lang). Model fit `r fit_verdict(fm_lang["cfi"], fm_lang["rmsea"])` (CFI $\geq$ .95, RMSEA $\leq$ .06) [@hu1999cutoff], CFI: `r round(fm_lang["cfi"], 3)`, RMSEA: `r round(fm_lang["rmsea"], 3)`, RMSEA p-value: 
`r pval_fmt(fitMeasures(fit_lang)["rmsea.pvalue"])`. Standardized loadings were moderate-to-strong: ROAR-Word = `r round(load_tab_lang["swr"], 2)`, ROAR-Sentence = `r round(load_tab_lang["sre"], 2)`, ROAR-Phoneme = `r round(load_tab_lang["pa"], 2)`, Sentence Understanding = `r round(load_tab_lang["trog"], 2)`, Vocabulary = `r round(load_tab_lang["vocab"], 2)`. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-semplot-lang
#| dependson: sem-lang-plot
#| fig-cap: "External validity evidence for Language: SEM including the ROAR tasks as external criterion measures.
#| *Note: The oval represents the latent factor and rectangles represent observed task scores. Green arrows show factor loadings. Values on paths are standardised coefficients.*"
#| fig-height: 4

plot_sem_clear(g_lang)
```

Because both domains span ages 5 to 13, convergence with an external criterion could in principle reflect nothing more than two developmentally sensitive measures rising together. We therefore refitted both models with age regressed on every indicator, so that each factor is estimated only from the variance remaining once age-related growth is removed from each task (@tbl-ext-agecontrol). The two specifications have the same degrees of freedom within each domain and so are directly comparable, and the age-controlled specification fits markedly better for executive function (`r ext_fit(fit_ef_c)`, versus `r ext_fit(fit_ef)`) and essentially the same for Language (`r ext_fit(fit_lang_c)`, versus `r ext_fit(fit_lang)`). For Language, all five loadings remain substantial, so its convergence with the ROAR measures is not an artifact of shared developmental growth. For executive function the loadings attenuate considerably, most of all for Hearts and Flowers; the MEFS loading falls but remains appreciable, indicating that executive function convergence is real but rests to a greater extent on age-related variance shared among its tasks. This control is deliberately conservative: across this age span, age-graded growth is part of the constructs themselves, so the age-controlled column is best read as a lower bound rather than a corrected estimate.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ext-agecontrol
#| dependson: sem-external-agecontrol
#| tbl-cap: "Standardised factor loadings for the external-validity models with and without an age control. *Note: The age-controlled specification regresses age on every indicator, so each factor is estimated from the variance remaining after age-related growth is removed from each task. External criterion measures are marked.*"

ext_loadings |>
  flextable() |>
  autofit() |>
  merge_v(j = "Domain") |>
  align(j = c("Without age control", "With age control"), align = "center", part = "all") |>
  bold(j = "Domain", bold = TRUE, part = "body") |>
  valign(j = "Domain", valign = "top", part = "body")
```

### What the validity evidence establishes

Three conclusions follow, and we state them plainly because the pattern is mixed. First, the tasks measure *something* coherent and do so well: every loading in @fig-semplot-core-tasks is substantial and significant, and both external criteria converge on their intended factors. On the two questions a measures paper must answer -- do the tasks hang together, and do they agree with established instruments -- the answer is yes.

Second, overall fit falls short of conventional thresholds. We report this rather than respecifying the model to reach them. The residual covariance structure is reproduced reasonably well (SRMR = `r round(fitMeasures(fit_cov_age)["srmr"], 3)`), and the loadings are strong throughout, so the shortfall is not a failure of the individual tasks to measure their constructs. It does mean the three-factor structure imposed here is an imperfect account of how those constructs relate to one another -- which, together with the high inter-factor correlations, is why we defer that question to dedicated work rather than settling it from these data.

Third, the two external-validity models are not equally strong. Language coheres independently of age and converges with the ROAR measures, making it the best-evidenced construct in the battery. Executive Function is the weakest: its coherence rests substantially on age-related variance shared among its tasks, and its convergence with the MEFS is correspondingly less secure than the loading in @fig-semplot-ef implies when considered on its own. Strengthening the EF measures is the clearest priority for the next wave.

We regard this as the appropriate conclusion for a first pilot of a new battery: the measurement foundation is sound, the organisation of the constructs is left to dedicated work, and the specific weaknesses are identified rather than averaged away.

\clearpage

# Adaptive Task Construction

Adaptive administration serves the design principle of a feasible total duration. A battery of nine tasks intended to be completed in about an hour leaves only a few minutes per task, and a fixed form long enough to measure the full 5--12 range precisely is longer than that budget allows. Computer adaptive testing resolves the tension directly: by selecting items matched to each child's current ability estimate, it obtains comparable precision from far fewer items.

We have already adapted and piloted several of the LEVANTE core tasks as computer adapted versions, primarily in the mpieva-de and western-ca pilot sites. To date, these include Same & Different, Math, Pattern Matching, Shape Rotation, Sentence Understanding, and Vocabulary.  These adaptive versions of the tasks maintain an ability score, $\theta$, as an estimate of the participant's skill level that is updated at the end of each trial. This updated $\theta$ is then used to select an item best suited to their estimated ability, which both improves test-taker experience and yields more information on participant skill per item, allowing for a shorter task with fewer items. See @fig-age-trends-cat for age-related ability trends in the tasks currently using the adaptive format. 

The CAT tasks use an adaptive algorithm made available by the open source JavaScript library jsCat [@ma2025roar]. The present LEVANTE CAT implementation varies item difficulty and the lower asymptote -- the guessing floor introduced above -- while holding discrimination and the upper asymptote constant at 1; that is, items differ in difficulty and in the chance of success from guessing, but not in how sharply they discriminate between ability levels. Items are selected by maximum Fisher information, that is, by choosing the item whose response is most informative at the child's current ability estimate. Within a CAT session $\theta$ is updated by maximum likelihood, bounded at -6 and 6; this differs from the expected a posteriori (EAP) estimator used for the fixed-form scores reported elsewhere in this paper, which draws on a population prior that is not available mid-session. The LEVANTE CATs are configurable with respect to the initial value of theta and the conditions for ending the task. The starting $\theta$ is set at 0 for all CAT tasks currently in use, but could in principle be set according to the researcher's prior expectation of participant ability, for example, by using age as a proxy indicator of the initial ability estimate.

Current CAT implementations use time-based stopping rules to facilitate group assessment so that all children end at approximately the same time. Sentence Understanding, Shape Rotation, and Vocabulary each have time limits currently set to 4 minutes. Pattern Matching was set to 6 minutes to allow for the increased time typically required to complete items in this task. Items in these tasks are presented together in a single block. 

Same and Different and Math are each divided into three blocks presented sequentially, with per-block stopping based on number of items. These CATs select from the list of items specific to their current block and proceed to the next block once the target number of items is reached, maintaining one $\theta$ estimate for the entire task. Same and Different and Math have time limits of 6 minutes and 8 minutes, respectively. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-trends-cat
#| fig-cap: "Age related trends by task for computer adaptive assessments."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

cat_only <- coretask_scores |> filter(adaptive)
cat_counts <- cat_only |> count(task_category, task)

ggplot(cat_only, aes(x = age, y = score)) +
  facet_nested_wrap(vars(task_category, task),
                    nest_line = element_line(), solo_line = TRUE,
                    axes = "x", scales = "free_y") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = site_label), alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = site_label, group = site_label),
              method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "re"), se = FALSE) +
  geom_label(data = cat_counts, inherit.aes = FALSE,
             aes(label = sprintf("N = %s", n)),
             x = Inf, y = -Inf, hjust = "inward", vjust = "inward",
             size = 3, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(6, 14, 2)) +
  .scale_colour_site() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = NA, linetype = 1, linewidth = 2))) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Ability (IRT score)", colour = "Site") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Standard errors of IRT ability estimates were generally comparable across adaptive and fixed-length versions; typical SE ≈ 0.4–0.8 (see @fig-se in appendices). In most tasks, the fixed-length forms yielded slightly lower SEs than the adaptive forms across the mid to high range of ability, whereas adaptive forms showed marginally lower SEs for a small number of children at the lowest ability levels. Given the small cell sizes in these extreme bands and the modest magnitude of differences, precision of ability estimates was broadly similar across administration modes. The gain is therefore in administration time rather than in precision. Median durations for the adaptive forms (@tbl-durations) ran at 38--59% of their fixed-form counterparts for five of the six adapted tasks -- Vocabulary 38%, Shape Rotation 40%, Math 44%, Sentence Understanding 48% and Same & Different 59% -- with Pattern Matching the exception at 94%, reflecting the longer time its items require. Comparable precision from roughly half the testing time is the practical case for adaptive administration.

# General Discussion

In this paper, we presented the LEVANTE core tasks -- nine psychometrically grounded tasks for children aged 5–12 that assess language, mathematics, reasoning, executive function, and social cognition abilities. LEVANTE is designed to tackle three core challenges: to span development and enable valid comparisons between younger and older children; to ensure cross-cultural comparability so that measures function equivalently across diverse contexts; and to make the tasks openly available (non-commercial) to maximize access, transparency, and reproducibility.

## Current status of the core tasks

Using pilot data from four sites on three continents, collected via three different administration methods (in-school, in-lab, and at-home administration), we provided preliminary evidence of developmental sensitivity, reliability, and validity. Further, using computer adaptive testing algorithms, we are able to deploy efficient versions of these tasks that produce scores for children across a wide range of abilities in a median of three to six minutes per task. While these tasks do not all yet meet conventional thresholds for reliability, it is important to note that they still fill a gap. Many tasks commonly used to measure these constructs with children have never been assessed for reliability and may well be substantially less reliable than those presented here. 

It is also worth situating our measurement-invariance results within the broader developmental measurement literature. Although measurement invariance has received substantial attention in large longitudinal panel studies and data-harmonization efforts [e.g. @widaman2010factorial], formal tests remain less common for children's cognitive task batteries, and tests spanning tests spanning different administration modes, languages, and cultural contexts rarer still [@putnick2016]. Against this backdrop, our finding that most LEVANTE tasks reach scalar invariance across four sites that differ substantially in sampling, language, and mode of administration is a comparatively strong result: it suggests that cross-site score differences are more likely attributable to genuine sample and administration differences than to non-equivalent measurement, and that the LEVANTE scale supports pooling data across highly heterogeneous data-collection contexts. Where invariance did not hold, this is itself informative, flagging specific tasks or item types that may need further localization.

<!-- ToDo: update language: are we done revising tasks? have we met more of our reliability criteria? mention that Vocab likely does vary by language, and maybe Stories is reasonable, too (linguistic + cultural differences?) -->
We continue to refine several of the nine tasks, and we expect gains in reliability and validity as items are refined, distractors improved, and instructions localized. We are actively monitoring task performance and iteratively refining items as new data accrue across sites. This includes updating IRT calibrations, conducting routine checks for differential item functioning, and making revisions guided by fit diagnostics and error patterns. These are the ordinary maintenance practices of high-stakes testing programmes, which recalibrate and screen items for bias as a matter of routine; what is unusual here is not the procedures themselves but that they are being applied to openly licensed research measures and reported publicly. We are attempting to strike a balance between minimizing bias and ensuring that observed differences reflect genuine variation rather than artifacts of the measurement process.
With pilot data collection complete, our goal here has been to present the LEVANTE framework tasks, our scoring methods, and an initial analysis of validity and reliability. Although task refinement is an iterative process, we discuss the next steps of extending the framework for broader participation in data collection and analysis.

## Limitations

Because the pilot sites (and future LEVANTE study sites) differ widely in processes of sampling, recruitment, and administration, any differences in absolute performance across sites are confounded. 
Thus, absolute performance differences across sites cannot and should not be interpreted. 
Moreover, because the LEVANTE tasks were under active development during the pilot study, the data reported here could be expected to exhibit greater variability than future LEVANTE studies -- including across-site differences, as data collection at uniandes-co-bogota preceded the other sites.

A further limitation concerns the origin of the task content. The core tasks were authored in English and
subsequently adapted into Spanish and German, rather than being developed concurrently across languages.
Although the adaptation process involved native-speaker researchers at each site, and although items were
selected and illustrated with cross-cultural interpretability in mind, the conceptual framing of the tasks
nonetheless originates in an English-speaking context. Material that seems unremarkable to an English-speaking designer may be unfamiliar elsewhere, and
translation changes the wording of an item rather than what it is about. Developing items concurrently with partner sites, rather than adapting them outward from an English
original, is a priority as the network expands.

A further limitation concerns the longitudinal evidence. Repeat administrations were available at a single site, and the interval between them ran from roughly three to seven months rather than the days or weeks over which test-retest reliability is conventionally assessed. Over an interval that long, and at ages when the abilities measured are changing quickly, the retest correlations confound the stability of the measure with genuine developmental change, and three tasks were additionally retested with newly written items. They are therefore better read as evidence of rank-order stability across a developmentally meaningful period than as reliability coefficients.

Another limitation of this study is that external validation evidence was available only for the executive function and language/literacy domains, where LEVANTE scores could be compared against existing standardized measures (MEFS; the ROAR battery). For Math, Reasoning, and Social Cognition, we report internal (construct) validity and developmental sensitivity, but lack an external benchmark against which to assess convergent validity. Identifying suitable comparison measures across our target languages and age range for these domains is an important direction for future work, as is establishing where these measures sit in the larger nomological net of measures and constructs.

Given the preliminary nature of this validation, we highlight several limitations on the current use of LEVANTE scores. First, calibrations reported here should not be used to draw conclusions about absolute differences between the specific sites studied. Second, task content and item parameters remain under active revision; researchers using these tasks should consult the LEVANTE repository for the current item bank and calibration before drawing on results reported here. Third, given the preliminary state of the reliability and validity evidence, we do not recommend using individual LEVANTE scores for high-stakes, individual-level decisions (e.g., clinical or educational placement).

## Future directions

Our plan is for the core tasks presented here to become the backbone of the LEVANTE framework, in which sites around the world collaborate to collect longitudinal data measuring children's learning and development as well as the overlapping contexts in which these children develop. De-identified data collected using the tasks presented here flow into a shared repository, becoming part of a large-scale dataset that we hope will enable a wide variety of downstream investigations. The power of these data is that -- especially when combined with contextual data about children's caregivers, home environment, school, and community environment -- they allow analysis of the sources of developmental and contextual variability at global scale.

Towards this goal, one strength of our approach here is that it easily accommodates future internationalization and adaptation. In fact, at the time of writing we are working on adaptations for two more languages (French and Dutch) and we intend to further broaden the set of languages for which the tasks are available. As part of this process, we have created a website for generating and reviewing translation materials. The LEVANTE researcher website documents the use of this platform and our ongoing language adaptation efforts: <https://researcher.levante-network.org>. 

Our current task set is designed for children ages 5--12, but we are currently pursuing downward extension of many of these tasks for children ages 2--4. By design, the forced choice, tablet-based format of our tasks makes them highly amenable to use with younger children [@frank2016]. In our downward extension work, we are adding easier items to each task, increasing the number of practice trials, and increasing the amount of instructions. We anticipate that not all tasks will be usable for all ages, but for at least the executive function and language tasks there is strong evidence of usability with children under age 5 [@davidson2006;@bishop1982;@long_ma_tan_silverman_frank_yeatman_2025]. 

## Conclusions

In sum, we have taken steps here towards creating a core set of tasks for measuring children's learning and development. We hope that this work is the beginning, rather than the end, of a process of iterative refinement and growth that results in a common, open measurement toolkit for developmental science.

# Bifactor and Schmid-Leiman analysis of the core task battery {.appendix #apx-bifactor}

Given the very high inter-factor correlations reported in the Construct Validity section, we investigated whether a bifactor structure -- a single general factor alongside domain-specific factors -- might better characterize the data. Unlike the main SEM in @fig-semplot-core-tasks, Math and Stories are treated here as indicators of the Reasoning and Language factors respectively, rather than as separate outcomes; this is the specification a bifactor decomposition requires, since every task must load on the general factor. Fit indices in this appendix are therefore not directly comparable with those in the main text.

{{\< include _09-bifactor.qmd \>}}

--- main-text paragraph that summarised it (sat in Construct Validity) ---
Given these high inter-factor correlations, we investigated whether a bifactor structure (i.e., a single general factor alongside domain-specific factors) might better characterize the data; see Appendix for the full analysis. That analysis uses its own specification, in which Math and Stories load on the Reasoning and Language factors rather than standing as separate outcomes, because a bifactor decomposition requires every task to load on the general factor; its fit indices are therefore not directly comparable with those reported here. A direct bifactor model produced an improper (Heywood-case) solution (@tbl-bifactor-fit-compare), which can have several possible causes (e.g., sampling variability or too few indicators per specific factor), but the pattern here converges with the model-free implied loadings (see Appendix: @tbl-analytic-g-loadings), consistent with specific factors carrying little variance beyond a dominant general factor. We therefore recovered general- and specific-factor loadings via a second-order model with a Schmid-Leiman transformation [@schmid1957development] (@tbl-bifactor-methods-comparison). Reasoning proved essentially indistinguishable from a general factor, while Executive Function and especially Language retained modestly more distinguishable variance. Explained common variance (ECV = .91) and omega-hierarchical ($\omega_{H}$ = .88) both exceeded conventional thresholds for treating the battery as substantially general-factor-dominated in practice [@reise2012rediscovery; @rodriguez2016evaluating] (@tbl-bifactor-indices), though our inter-factor correlations run higher than comparable estimates from a twin sample of Texas children (Reasoning–EF *r* = .84, EF–Language *r* = .76, Reasoning–Language *r* = .75; [@engelhardt2016]), particularly for Language. We note that comparative fit is not the basis for this characterization; bifactor models are known to exhibit elevated fitting propensity [@bonifay2017complexity; @bonifay2025reassessing], and our reading rests on the model-free implied loadings and variance-partitioning indices reported in Appendix A rather than on the fit comparison in Table A1.

# Site-imbalance robustness check {#apx-subsample}

Sample sizes are imbalanced across the pilot sites (see Data filtering), which raises the concern that the correlated three-factor model's high inter-factor correlations could be an artifact of pooling over unevenly-sized, unevenly-composed sites rather than a genuine feature of the tasks. We evaluate this directly with two complementary checks: repeatedly refitting the three-factor model on equal-size-per-site subsamples, and refitting it separately within each individual site (no cross-site pooling at all). The full-sample estimates fell at or within the 95% interval of these robustness analyses.

{{< include _10-subsample-robustness.qmd >}}

# Precision of ability estimates {.appendix #apx-irt-se}

```{r}
#| label: fig-se
#| fig-cap: "Standard error of IRT ability estimates by ability level for fixed-length versus adaptive versions of the six CAT tasks."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

# tasks that have CAT versions 
tasks_cat <- cat_only |> distinct(task, task_category)

ability_scores_cat <- coretask_scores |>
  semi_join(tasks_cat, by = c("task", "task_category")) |>
  mutate(adaptive = if_else(adaptive, "Non-adaptive", "Adaptive (CAT)"))

ggplot(ability_scores_cat,
       aes(x = score, y = score_se, colour = adaptive)) +
  facet_nested_wrap(vars(task_category, task),
                    nest_line = element_line(), solo_line = TRUE,
                    axes = "x", scales = "free_y") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam") +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  # scale_colour_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Ability (IRT score)", y = "Standard error of ability",
       colour = "Administration method") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
